name: Espresso (Double)
description: The foundation of the café menu: a short, syrupy shot with a hazelnut-coloured crema on top.

steps.text: Grind 18 g of coffee fine — a little finer than table salt — into a dry portafilter.
Level the bed with a tap or finger, then tamp firmly and evenly.
Lock in the portafilter, put a cup on the scale and start the shot straight away.
Stop when about 36 g of liquid is in the cup. This should take roughly 25–30 seconds.
Taste. Sour and fast? Grind finer. Bitter and slow? Grind coarser. Change one thing at a time.

tips: Time is a diagnostic, not a target — taste decides.
Warm the cup first so the shot doesn't cool instantly.

sources.name: La Marzocco Home — Using espresso brew ratios
Podium Coffee Club — Espresso brew ratio explained

name: Ristretto
description: A 'restricted' shot — the same dose as an espresso but pulled shorter, for a sweeter, denser sip.

steps.text: Dose, level and tamp 18 g of finely ground coffee just as for a normal espresso.
Start the shot and cut it early, at about 20–27 g in the cup (roughly 15–20 seconds).
Serve immediately — it's gone in two or three sips.

tips: A ristretto is the traditional base for a piccolo latte.

sources.name: Bean Box — Espresso drink menu translated
Pro Coffee Gear — Coffee drinks chart

name: Lungo
description: A 'long' shot: more water pushed through the same puck for a bigger, lighter-bodied and more bitter cup.

steps.text: Prepare the portafilter with 18 g of coffee, ground a touch coarser than for espresso.
Pull the shot until you have around 54 g in the cup, about 35–45 seconds.
Stir the crema in and drink hot.

tips: Unlike an americano, all the water in a lungo passes through the coffee.

sources.name: Pro Coffee Gear — Coffee drinks chart

name: Caffè Americano
description: Espresso lengthened with hot water — the body of filter coffee with espresso's roasty depth.

steps.text: Pull a double espresso (about 36 g) into a large mug.
Top up with 150–200 ml of hot water, adjusting to taste.
Give it a stir and serve.

tips: Water poured on top breaks up the crema — that's the key difference from a long black.

sources.name: Trade Coffee — Americano vs long black

name: Long Black
description: The Aussie/Kiwi take on an americano: water first, espresso on top, so the crema stays intact.

steps.text: Pour about 100 ml of hot water into a small (120–180 ml) cup.
Pull a double espresso directly on top of the water.
Serve without stirring so the crema floats on the surface.

tips: Less water than an americano, so it tastes more intense.

sources.name: Sage Appliances — Long black vs americano
Hoxton Coffee Co — Americano vs long black

name: Affogato
description: A scoop of vanilla ice cream 'drowned' in a hot shot of espresso. Dessert and coffee in one glass.

steps.text: Chill a small glass or bowl in the freezer for a few minutes.
Add one or two firm scoops of vanilla ice cream (or gelato).
Pull a shot of espresso and pour it straight over the ice cream.
Grate a little chocolate over the top if you like and eat right away with a spoon.

tips: No espresso machine? A very strong moka pot or AeroPress shot works too.

sources.name: Inside The Rustic Kitchen — Italian affogato

name: Espresso Romano
description: Espresso served with a twist of lemon peel whose oils add a bright citrus lift.

steps.text: Use a peeler to take a thin strip of lemon peel, avoiding the bitter white pith.
Pull a shot of espresso into a demitasse.
Twist the peel over the cup to spray its oils on the surface, then rub it on the rim.
Drop the peel in or set it on the saucer and serve.

sources.name: Perfect Daily Grind — What is the espresso romano?

name: Espresso con Panna
description: A single or double espresso crowned with a dollop of whipped cream.

steps.text: If starting from heavy cream, whisk a few tablespoons to soft peaks.
Pull a shot of espresso into a small glass or demitasse.
Spoon the whipped cream on top and serve straight away.

sources.name: Starbucks at Home — Espresso con panna
